title: Blaise (3 February)
hookLine: a bishop who, in his story, saved a boy choking on a fishbone; throats are blessed with crossed candles

lines: A LINE AT THE FRONT OF CHURCH.
cards: Early February, a weekday Mass, and at the end a line forms at the front. One by one, people step up, and the priest holds two long candles, crossed in an X and tied with a ribbon, gently against each throat.
A short blessing, and they step aside. Kids giggle at the candles under their chins. Older people close their eyes.
Someone with a cold coughs and gets blessed anyway. It's a gentle, slightly strange custom, and it belongs to a bishop called Blaise.

teach.h: A BISHOP AND MARTYR OF SEBASTE.
teach.b: Blaise was a bishop of Sebaste, in Armenia, in the early centuries, and he died a martyr. That much the Church remembers. The rest comes from later stories, and the Church tells them as stories.
In the first, Blaise is being led away under arrest when a mother pushes through the crowd with her son. The boy has a fishbone stuck in his throat and can't breathe.
Blaise blesses him and prays, and the bone comes loose. The boy lives. In the second, a poor woman's only pig has been carried off by a wolf, and at Blaise's word the wolf gives it back.

teach.h: A WOMAN BRINGS CANDLES TO HIS CELL.
teach.b: Later, when Blaise is in prison, she comes to see him, bringing food and candles to light his cell. A throat, and candles: put them together and you get the custom.

On his feast, a priest or deacon holds two crossed candles at each person's throat and asks God, through the prayers of Saint Blaise, bishop and martyr, to free them from illness of the throat and from every other illness.

teach.h: A BLESSING IS A PRAYER, NOT A CHARM.
teach.b: The candles are not magic; in Catholic teaching a blessing is a prayer, not a charm. It puts a whole body, the part that swallows and speaks and sings, into God's hands for a moment.
The Church prays a line from the Psalms at the start of each day in the Liturgy of the Hours.

teach.h: O LORD, THOU WILT OPEN MY LIPS.
teach.b: In the Douay-Rheims: "O Lord, thou wilt open my lips: and my mouth shall declare thy praise." A throat, opened, for praise.

how: On Saint Blaise's feast, Catholic parishes often offer the blessing of throats, with a priest or deacon holding two crossed candles at each person's throat while saying the blessing.

games.q: you're Blaise, under arrest and being led away. a mother pushes through the crowd: her son is choking on a fishbone. what do you do?
o: keep walking; the guards won't stop.
bless the boy and pray for him.
tell her to find a doctor.
games.why: in the story he blessed and prayed over the boy, and the bone came loose. it's why throats are blessed on his day.

practice: Notice your own throat for a moment, the swallow, the air moving through, then bring to mind someone whose throat hurts or whose voice is struggling: a friend with a cold, a teacher who's lost their voice, someone who finds it hard to swallow.
If you pray, ask Saint Blaise to pray for them and say the psalm line, O Lord, open my lips; if you don't, wish them ease and a clear voice.
